Good morning, Excellencies and distinguished delegates, and welcome back to the last plenary meeting of the 2025 Annual Session of the UN Women Executive Board. Let us now continue our consideration of Item 10 on policy and program matters, during which the Executive Board will receive 3 different presentations, including A briefing on UN Women's operational response in Europe and Central Asia, an update on the implementation of General Assembly Resolution 72/279 on the repositioning of the United Nations Development System, and an update on UN Women policies and procedures to tackle sexual exploitation and abuse and sexual harassment. Let's now turn to the first presentation, the briefing on UN Women's operational response in Europe and Central Asia. In addition to the Executive Director, Deputy Executive Directors, and the Executive Board Secretary, allow me to welcome the following colleagues to the podium: Shoko Ishikawa, Deputy Director, Program Policy and Intergovernmental Division, and Belén Sanz-Luc, Regional Director of Europe and Central Asia, joining us remotely. And now I'm pleased to invite Mrs. Belén Sanz-Luc, Regional Director for Europe and Central Asia, for her presentation.

Please. Thank you very much, Madam President of the Executive Board, Ms. Nicola Klaas, Excellencies, and UN Women colleagues. I would like, on behalf of the Regional Office for Europe and Central Asia, to thank the Board Secretariat for the opportunity to present UN Women's operational response across Europe and Central Asia in this very important annual session of the Executive Board. The purpose of my presentation is to outline and exemplify how UN Women translates its triple mandate into meaningful results for women and girls across Europe and Central Asia. I'd like to remind that in May 2024, we had the honor of receiving an Executive Board delegation to Ukraine and Moldova, where the Board had the opportunity to witness firsthand the deployment of our triple mandate and our engagement with different partners. Thank you to the Board for undertaking that visit. If we move to the second slide, please. The Europe and Central Asia region is a large and diverse region with respect to economic development, political systems, rights protection, culture, religion, and also vulnerability to natural hazards. Many of the countries in the region experience complex legacies of political and economic transition and significant development efforts. I'd like to underline that UN Women's universal mandate guides our normative engagement with 56 member states of the UN Economic Commission for Europe, of which we work operationally with 18 countries in line with the United Nations presence across the region. Our triple mandate is implemented from UN Women Regional Office based and hosted in Istanbul, Türkiye, and its UN Women offices across 3 sub-regions: the Western Balkans, and Türkiye, South Caucasus and Eastern Partnership countries, and Central Asia. Next slide, please. I'd like to reflect that although the geopolitical context remains fluid in the region and there is still the affection of, of course, global uncertainty, which in some cases has seen a stagnation in some progress on results, countries have continued to advance commitments to gender equality. To the empowerment and rights of women and girls. To give some examples, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Moldova, Bosnia-Herzegovina have introduced recently legislations to tackle violence against women. Albania amended the electoral code in 2024, establishing a 30% electoral quota, and Uzbekistan established a 40% electoral quota in 2023, which has resulted in notable women's representation in parliament. Of 33%. Tajikistan has issued a decree reducing the number of professions where women were legally barred, and Ukraine has passed gender laws despite the ongoing full-scale war. Next slide, please. Across the region, gains have also been recorded in women's participation and representation in political and public life. Between 2000 and 2024, the share of seats held by women in national parliaments more than tripled, with 27% of seats in national parliaments, an increase from 19% in 2015. Women are best represented in local governments in the Eastern Partnership countries with 38%, and followed by the Western Balkans with 33%. In spite of this notable progress, what the data tell us, including through our recently launched Gender Snapshot, is that no country in Europe and Central Asia is fully on track to achieve gender equality by 2030. We need sustained political will investments now more than ever to deliver on Agenda 2030 and for achieving the commitment that countries have for gender equality in this region. Next slide, please. The progress in the region has not been uniform. Despite relatively high educational attainment among women in many countries in Europe and Central Asia, structural barriers remain to women's full free and equal participation. Some data indicate to us that there is a consistent gender gap of 25% in labor force participation. Women devote 3.4 times as much time to unpaid care work, and the gender pay gap averages 20%, though it varies widely across countries. And one signal of the structural barriers indicate that women are 2.5 times more likely to be in vulnerable forms of employment than men. With regards to violence against women, this remains high and underreported among many of the countries. Over a period of 12 months, 24 million women have experienced physical or sexual violence by their partner, and technology-facilitated violence is on the rise. With significant reports from women and girls across the region. If we move to the next slide, please. We cannot underline more than enough how the persistence and escalation of armed conflict in the region, most notably Russia's full-scale war in Ukraine, but also crises and conflicts in neighboring regions, continue to have a profound impact on gender equality, on women's rights, and also on regional peace and stability. These crises have disproportionately affected women and girls, and only in Ukraine, 3.6 million people remain internally displaced, of which 80% are women and children. Another growing concern that we are observing in the region is related to the backlash against gender equality and some erosion of the civic space, where many countries across the region have seen the emergence or consolidation of movements that are opposing gender equality and are challenging the legitimacy of international human rights standards. Next slide, please. I'd like to move to presenting the key results achieved across Europe and Central Asia over the last strategic note period, 2021-2025, based on our triple mandate. I'd like to underscore that at the normative level, UN Women's central role has been focused on setting and advancing normative standards with our key UN and national partners on gender equality, including through intergovernmental processes. This includes leading and supporting normative work on key international frameworks. Some key highlights from this work include the regional review meeting and report that was undertaken with the UNEC, where 95% of countries produced a National Report on Beijing+30. Can we move to the next slide, please? In our work on operational response, our first cluster of support focuses on gender-responsive governance. This includes strengthening women's leadership and political participation, working on gender-responsive budgeting, strengthening statistical systems to improve the availability and use of gender-sensitive data, and also supporting the accession countries to the European Union to integrate gender equality across all aspects of the integration and accession process. We have supported to increase the women's political representation and influence through our support and strategies with national partners, and we have deployed robust efforts in investing in gender-responsive budgeting, including at the national and local frameworks. Finally, in this very important area of gender governance, We have invested hand in hand and with other UN agencies in gender data systems to enable a better tracking of progress on SDG 5 and inform evidence-based policymaking, particularly in 3 critical areas: violence against women, unpaid care work, and femicide. In the next slide, I'd like to highlight how the Women, Peace and Security Agenda has advanced in the region significantly with regards to our engagement with 14 countries out of the 17 with whom we have direct interaction through their National Action Plans, and 82% of the UN Economic Commission for Europe countries have a National Action Plan. In Moldova, UN Women has supported community-based initiatives and advocacy for women's inclusion in peace processes, and almost 8,000 individuals, primarily women, including 2,000 refugees from Ukraine, enhance their employability through skills training, leadership engagement, and integration activities. And we have increased also our capacity to respond in humanitarian settings, including in Türkiye after the devastating earthquake, with whom we supported 15,000 women and girls to receive essential services as earthquake response and recovery. Next slide, please. On ending violence against women, institutions across Europe and Central Asia have advanced the implementation of the Istanbul Convention, and UN Women has supported integrated programming contributing to more survivor-centered accountability. Over 27 million people have been reached through our advocacy campaigns to address and transform gender stereotypes and For example, 6 countries such as Tajikistan, Ukraine, Kazakhstan, Moldova, Georgia, and Bosnia and Herzegovina took deliberate action to improve the legislative environment for violence against women. On women's economic empowerment, in 2024, 6.2 million people were reached through our outreach campaigns, and 5 countries— Albania, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Georgia, Serbia, and Moldova— implemented reforms on care work, including very interesting examples from Kyrgyzstan introducing home-based childcare and a care voucher system, and Moldova introducing alternative childcare facilities at the workplace, and Serbia piloting innovative services like Octopus for rural women. In the next slide, I would like to highlight that all the work we undertake in the region is done in collaboration and coordination with the UN system, which we have strengthened over the last period by leveraging our triple mandate. We have worked hand in hand with the Resident Coordinators and the UN Country Teams, supporting the cooperation frameworks over this period and exceeding standards of the UNCT SWAP indicators in the region. 65% of the existing cooperation frameworks mainstream gender equality across all outcomes. And across the region, over 38% of our ongoing programs are implemented with other UN agencies, And in Kyrgyzstan and Bosnia and Herzegovina, 100% of our programs are implemented together with other UN agencies. At the regional level, we work closely with regional-level UN organizations, including with UNDP, with UNFPA, with UNEC, DCO, and other important sister agencies. And at the regional level, our role is very much to support and pivot to the countries work and also look at challenges that transcend national borders in order to advocate for regional integration, coherence, and joint solutions to issues that affect multiple countries, including through the generation of substantive knowledge, data, and policy influence. To move into the operational side of our work— and I'm coming to the end, Madam Chair— we have as a region implemented over the last 4-year period $190 million throughout the region, of which 17% have been core resources and 83% non-core funding. Nearly 70% of the total core resources have been allocated to country offices, ensuring the flexible needs-based support for a strategic note implementation in line with national gender equality agendas. In addition to these, the strategic notes direct funding by a number, an increasing number of funding partners, including in Albania, Georgia, Moldova, and Ukraine, have supported our country offices to have flexible, demand-driven, and impactful interventions in the different countries. Our non-core resources have increased through the generosity and commitment of our partners by 28% over the period 2022-2024. I would like to thank the— in this opportunity, our funding partners for their very important contributions in the region, including the European Union, Sweden, Denmark, Austria, Norway, Switzerland, UK, Italy, Canada, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan as host countries. And we also deeply thank the national committees in our region. We are exploring diversifying the sources of funding and fostering partnerships with the private sector, with the IFIs, including further government co-sharing contributions. And we have invested in this period to ensure compliance with accountability frameworks, including the undertaking of an internal audit, a functional review of the regional work, and over 20 evaluations of our programs and country-level work. I finish saying that we are in the moment of finalizing our existing strategic note and reform— and informing now our upcoming regional strategic note in line with the global strategic plan that is under consultation right now. We are developing a forward-looking and fit-for-purpose regional strategic note, including through the development of foresight and systems thinking that ensures proof of strategy that of course takes into account the SGs UN80 initiative and that seeks to optimize efficiencies and joint collaboration at sub-regional and regional level. We have undertaken a number of consultations, including a recent consultation with a number of member states in Copenhagen. Where we have received significant inputs about the focus areas of our work, including of course the increased focus on digitalization, humanitarian action, and the work with men and boys to support our thematic areas. With this, I would like to end my presentation, and thank you, Madam Chair and Excellencies, for your attention and for all your support. Thank you very much.

Thank you very much, Belen. And I now open up the floor for member states' interventions with respect to the aforementioned briefing. And I give the floor now to the distinguished representative of Moldova.

Excellencies, distinguished colleagues, I would like to start by acknowledging and appreciating the important activities of the UN Women, with whom the Government of the Republic of Moldova had had— has had a long and fruitful cooperation. We appreciate the activity of the country office, which delivers on its triple mandate and provides among its various activities technical assistance on the normative amendment amendments and leads the country team to increase accountability towards gender equality. In connection with today's topic, I would like to highlight our ongoing collaboration with the UN Women in Moldova, conducted under the operational mandate to promote gender equality and the empowerment of women. This partnership continues to make a visible impact across several key areas. Notably, it supports women leadership in and participation in governance, monitors the instances of violence against women in politics, and assists the government in mainstreaming gender into policymaking and budgeting purposes— processes. The UN Women Country Office also works closely with both the government and the private sector to enhance women's economic participation. This includes support for business development programs, the promotion of alternative childcare solutions in the workplace, and initiatives to encourage the involvement of women and girls in STEM fields. In addition, UN Women activities support civil actively supports civil society organizations and offers expert guidance to the newly established Gender-Based Violence Agency, operational since 2024. This cooperation has shown tangible results and we are confident in its further development. Distinguished delegates, despite multiple challenges that Moldova has faced— has been facing in the last few years, the humanitarian crisis, the energy crisis, and the economic instability caused by Russia's war of aggression against Ukraine, the Republic of Moldova has strengthened its gender mechanism, improved legislation, and promoted politics for an equitable and resilient society. The national institution framework in Moldova consists of a new— of a network of government and private sector institutions and mechanisms tasked with implementing gender mainstreaming, addressing cases of gender-based discrimination, and monitoring the implementation of the CEDAW and Istanbul Conventions. The Republic of Moldova reached a historic milestone in 2025 by ranking 7th globally in the World Economic Forum's Global Gender Gap Index, making substantial national progress in closing the gender gap. This is the first time our country has entered the top 10, positioning us among the global leaders in gender equality. The most significant gains were achieved in the area of political empowerment, where the increased participation of women in decision-making roles led to women's representation raising to 42.5% in 2025. This represents a threefold increase in our score in this category since 2006, when the index was first introduced. This trend is also evident in the Moldovan government and in our judiciary system, where nearly half of the state secretaries and and Secretary-General positions are held by women, and more than half of all judges are women. I would like also to point some of the core successes recorded in '24. First, the introduction of the notion of femicide in our legislation, and we have expanded services to victims and survivors of sexual violence in all regions of the country. Establishment of a government agency for prevention and combating domestic violence and violence against women, expansion of services for survivors of violence. Establishment of a national coordination council for GBV and the GBV agency, enhancing oversight or alignment with the Istanbul Convention. Ratification of ILO 190 Convention on Elimination of Sexual Harassment at the Workplace, and many more. And here at the UN, we played an active role in Commission CSW 69, including in the negotiations of the Political Declaration 2025. Excellencies, these achievements reflect the long-term commitment and reinforced efforts of the Moldovan government and civil society, along with support from their international partners, to build a more inclusive society where women and men have equal, equal opportunities in public and professional life. The path to gender equality is not without difficulties, and process can feel slow at times, but by being united, governments international organizations, the civil society, and the private sector, we become a force for change. In this regard, our government is determined to work further to ensure gender equality, to combat the persistent gender norms and stereotypes, especially in the rural areas, and to eliminate all kinds of violence against women, including violence against women in politics, cases of hate speech, sexist speech, and smearing campaign recorded during elections. Together, with solidarity and empathy, we can make further progress and build a future where all have equal rights and opportunities, where everyone can fully realize their potential.

I thank the distinguished representative from the Republic of Moldova for his comments. And I now have 2 more speakers on my list, Sweden and the Federation of Russia. I now give the floor to the distinguished representative from Sweden.

Thank you, Madam President, for giving me the floor. And also thank you, Ms. Belenzans-Luke, for the update. And all of our congratulations to you and your team for your work helping member states turn global gender equality commitments into national actions. In May, Sweden welcomed Belén Sanz Luque and her team to Stockholm. They shared positive news about UN Women's work to boost women's leadership and political participation in Europe and Central Asia. Sweden strongly supports UN Women in the region with flexible strategic note funding, program funding, and political backing. And values the close cooperation between UN Women and our missions in the region.

I have a question.

In the context of rapidly changing global environments, with shrinking civic space and fiscal constraints on the multilateral system, how will UN Women articulate and deliver on its triple mandate, particularly its operational mandate? across Europe and Central Asia.

Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative from Sweden for her comments, and I now give the floor to the distinguished representative from the Russian Federation.

Thank you, Chair. We thank UN Women for presenting the report on activities in Eastern Europe and Central Asia. As is known, the situation in the region currently is extremely tense, and we thank this entity for its efforts to improve the situation of women and children in our region, especially those in vulnerable situations. At the same time, we call on UN Women in its reports to adhere to the principle of neutrality and not to use politicized language, such as, for example, the full scale Russian invasion of Ukraine, as written in the report.

This is repeated by today's rapporteur.

UN Women is an important specialized body for achieving gender equality and for empowering women. We're always prepared to work together with UN Women on specialized topics, including in the context of the upcoming 25th anniversary of Resolution 1325 on Women, Peace and Security. However, this one-sided assessment of our special military operation by UN Women does not at all help to establish constructive cooperation. Therefore, we once again call on you in the future to show restraint and neutrality in your assessment of the situation and to pay more attention to improving the situation of women. Thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative from the Russian Federation for his comments. And I have no further speakers on my list, so I therefore ask the Secretariat to respond.

Thank you, thank you, Madam President, on the report that we have presented and The comments from the member states, we want to appreciate the delegate from Moldova, and I will request my colleague Belén and our Deputy Director for Policy and Programme to provide further details and to appreciate also the comment from Sweden on how we seek to operate on the triple mandate in Europe and Central Asia in the context of the complexities and resource constraints that we have. Indeed, it's a comment to us and equally to the member states as you— to get directions from yourselves, as the last 2 days we have continued to affirm the triple mandate, and for us it's very important, the issue of impact in our countries and in communities. And we have noted the comment from Russia. Thank you very much, Madam President. I would like to defer to my colleagues, Madam Belén and Madam Shoko Ishikawa.

Thank you very much, Madam Chair and Deputy Executive Director. Thank you to member states for their comments and questions. I will refer directly to the question posed by the delegation of Sweden. Thank you very much for your support, but also for your question about how to ensure our operational support also in view of the current challenges that we are all facing in the region and globally. First of all, I would like to say that this is a region where we have seen, as I presented in my report, very important articulation between the United Nations sister agencies and UN Women, and we foresee that in the upcoming UN system cooperation frameworks, which are 12 countries under development, to ensure that these cooperation frameworks include a strong commitment to gender equality and women's rights and empowerment. And through this, we are already in close collaboration with the sister agencies in terms of deploying joint initiatives to respond to the gender equality challenges. In addition to this, we are working very closely in evaluating the programs that we have implemented in the different countries, and we have seen that it is extremely important to bring in an integrated manner our integrated triple mandate. And through our programs, we are bringing to the countries, and in support and partnership with the countries, the normative frameworks, uh, and informing these normative frameworks also from the national level, as well as leveraging our coordination response. So we do see that our forthcoming strategic note will strengthen our operational response, anchoring it very much in the UN coordination and normative mandate. And we do hope to build on the very strong examples that are being led by our countries with whom we work, including Moldova, who presented the very important strides that have been done on gender equality, and for which we really are very happy to see the increase of women's representation and many other areas that have been advanced in the country. So we do hope to engage also member states in the region as we tailor our operational response, building on the evaluations that we have undertaken and elevating our operational response in the context of our triple mandate.

Thank you very much. I have very little to add to what Belén has mentioned, but one thing that I would mention is that our triple mandate is really all 3 packaged in one, in a sense. So, for us to continue to be strong and agile and focused on our operational mandate, It is essential, and we are doing so in terms of stepping up on our coordination mandate, working hand in hand with the other UN agencies on identifying joint programming opportunities, also influencing how the joint programs are being formed, ensuring that gender is part of the operational activities of the other agencies. also is the way that we work on ensuring that the operational work of the UN system itself continues to deliver on women and girls. Thank you.

I thank the Secretariat for its response, and if there are no further comments or statements, we can move to the next presentation under this agenda item, namely an update on the implementation of General Assembly Resolution Resolution 72/279 on the repositioning of the United Nations Development System. In addition to the Executive Director, Deputy Executive Directors, and Executive Board Secretary, I welcome to the podium the following colleagues, namely Anna-Caren Jatfors, Director, Strategy, Planning, Resources and Effectiveness Division, and Alice Shackelford, Deputy Director, UN System Coordination Division. Today's Today's update on the implementation of the General Assembly Resolution 72/279 on the repositioning of the United Nations Development System will be presented by Deputy Executive Director, Mrs. Nyeransai Gumbanwanda. Madam Deputy Executive Director, you have the floor.
Thank you, Madam President, and again, good morning, esteemed Board, delegates of UN Women, and colleagues, and good morning to my Executive Director.
Morning.

Before I begin with an update on our continued efforts in the implementation of UN repositioning mandates and provisions, I really want to take this opportunity to recognize and appreciate the adoption by the Member States last Tuesday of the ECOSOC Resolution E/2025/L014 on mainstreaming gender perspective into all policies and programs in the United Nations system. This resolution that you adopted— adopted by ECOSOC last week reaffirms the coordination mandate of UN Women, and indeed reaffirm the importance of the system-wide tools that we have developed, like the Sector-Wide Approach 3.0, which already incorporates 70% of the Gender Equality Acceleration Plan indicators. This significant achievement provides us clear guidance on the importance and value of systematically mainstreaming gender perspective across the United Nations system, with strong emphasis on coordination, on accountability, and sustainable resourcing led by UN Women to advance gender equality, the empowerment of all women and girls at every level, and at a time when such efforts are more critical than ever. Turning to my update, UN Women remains committed to supporting a reinvigorated resident coordinator system, and a new generation of UN country teams through our country and regional offices, as we have heard from our work in Europe and Central Asia. In line with our mandate to lead, coordinate, and promote gender equality accountability within the UN system, we provide crucial advisory and technical guidance to the UN country teams in their prioritization of gender equality and the empowerment of women. UN system coordination mechanisms are essential for prioritizing gender equality in ensuring UN actions are grounded in diverse country contexts. Towards this end, UN Women leads or co-leads gender theme groups and gender in humanitarian action working groups where we have a presence. And offers policy guidance and technical support elsewhere. These groups are further supported from our leadership engagement in multiple issue-based coalitions, our thematic advisors, and the regional collaborative platforms. At the global level, we lead the Global Interagency Network on Women and Gender Equality, addressing issues across mandate. We operate in full alignment with management and accountability framework. Our corporate strategic plan at the country level is integrated with the UNCT priorities and developed in cooperation with the resident coordinators. As part of consolidation of UN system reforms, we continue to engage in joint programming, as we have heard in the last session. In addition, we engage in dialogue with development partners, and work together around resource mobilization and funding compacts. The inclusion of mandatory gender equality marker in pooled funding mechanism elevates accountability and enhances collaborative initiative. As a result of longstanding partnership with UN Women and supported with the expertise across the system, the Secretary-General's Peacebuilding Fund allocated 43% of its approved allocations in 2024 towards gender-responsive peacebuilding, continuing the trend of exceeding its own gender funding marker and target of 30%. In 2022 to 2024, UN Women led the analysis and consultation in design of 6 out of 7 of the pilot countries, like in Niger, DRC, Guatemala, and Colombia. As stewards of global funding mechanisms, the UN Trust Fund to End Violence Against Women. We are also the stewards of the Women, Peace and Humanitarian Fund and the Healthy Initiative. This UN Women-led, UN Women-facilitated fund exemplifies interagency collaboration and advances the goals of the Global Compact to ensure flexible, long-term financing aligned to localization and resilience agendas, and we continue to engage with the Spotlight Initiative and are actively supporting the Spotlight 2.0. Let me turn to support— how we support entities and the SDGs-related interventions at the country level. In 2024, we supported 116 country teams, 20% more than the previous year, and 75 UN entities in their implementation of UNCTE and UN sector-wide approaches on gender equality, respectively. What is very interesting is that each year different heads of agencies, entities, and funds actually report and write to UN Women on the progress they've made. There is an accountability at heads of agencies level through and to UN Women on the progress that they have made, and this for us is is very important. We are also, in this work, seeing very tangible results in various regions. We have, as UN Women, working with other UN agencies on scaling up the care systems, the care policies, especially in Latin America. That has been work led by UN Women, but working with other UN agencies. In Africa, we have supported, together with other UN agencies, the advocacy leading to the adoption of the African Union Convention on the Elimination of Violence Against Women and Girls that was adopted last year. We also continue to engage within the SEEDS, the work with the Small Island Developing Nations, to ensure that gender equality was included in ABUS. That is work that we did together with other UN agencies and indeed the work in Central Asia and in Europe that has also been shared. UN Women's leadership is also important in critical cross-cutting issues, further advancing system-wide coherence on issues like disability inclusion, which is very critical and which, as member states, you have continued to raise. UN Women has been very active in championing gender-responsive disability inclusion across all UN programming. Our Global Task Team on Disability and Inclusion has dedicated communities of practice and systematic support to UN country teams in gender mainstreaming. We have also been active and very supportive to women, girls, and HIV and working closely as one of the co-sponsors And indeed, UNAIDS Secretariat reports to this board periodically on the progress. That is an example again of how we are leveraging the totality of the UN capabilities to deliver on the development goals. As Secretariat of the UN Secretary-General Systemwide Strategy on Gender Parity, we provide guidance to 140 entities. We also serve as Secretariat of the the SG Gender Equality Acceleration Plan, driving system-wide transformation, as you had also presented yesterday. Achieving greater efficiency and better business practices is also very important, and my colleague Didi Kesimadi can add further information on this. The reforms of the UN system, including in the current context, continue to strengthen our commitment in harmonizing business operations and lowering transaction costs. We continue to engage actively in multiple interagency business mechanisms, working to incorporate gender perspectives in business practices, such as in procurement and human resource. In some of the milestones we have reached, at least last year, is 90% country offices participating in business operations strategy. our use of the Global Shared Services and as a recipient, including for human resource management and treasury services, the co-location of over 72% of our offices in the UN common premises and 6 offices participating in back-office services. Excellencies, I reiterate UN Women's full commitment to reposition the UN system, demonstrating coherence integration, harmonization, and agility in adapting to challenging contexts. As we move forward, we continue to engage in UNAID, as the Executive Director indicated yesterday, leading the UN system contribution within UNAID for mainstreaming gender equality. We also continue to support the member states in the revitalization of CSW and the implementation of the Pact for the Future, and equally working together with the UN system as we prepare for CSW 70, which is focusing on access to justice. We look forward to working strongly together with colleagues for the high-level meeting on the 22nd of September as our heads of states gather to advance the work that we are doing on gender equality and taking forward the agenda action that we have. Developed as part of CSW69. Again, thank you, thank you very much. Thank you, Madam President.

Thank you very much, Madam Deputy Executive Director, for your comprehensive presentation. And I now open up the floor for member states' interventions. And the speaker, the first speaker on the list is the Netherlands, and currently the only speaker on the list. So I now give the floor to distinguished representative of the Netherlands.

Thank you, Madam President, and let me follow the good example of the DED in wishing the Executive Director a good morning. Morning. I deliver this statement on behalf of the following member states and observers: Albania, Australia, Austria, Belgium, Bulgaria, Canada, Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Georgia, Germany, Greece, Hungary, Iceland, Ireland, Japan, Luxembourg, New Zealand, Norway, Portugal, the Republic of Moldova, Slovakia, Spain, Sweden, Switzerland, Türkiye, the United Arab Emirates, the United Kingdom, the EU as a donor, and my own country, the Kingdom of the Netherlands. Madam President, Madam Executive Director, colleagues, we are pleased to see the United Nations Development System reform is showing results. The UN, however, is operating in a context of growing demands and declining resources. This makes full implementation of UNDS reform indispensable to rebuild trust in the UN system and safeguard its global legitimacy. Ongoing reforms must continue with urgency and ambition. We welcome the Secretary-General's UN80 initiative and see clear opportunities to consolidate the learning and gains of the UNDS reform. We must ensure that the UN80 initiative builds on and not bypasses the reforms already underway. We would like to emphasize the following points. First, in light of persisting funding constraints, we see great potential in the further consolidation and increased use of shared services common back offices, and common premises. These are not just essential for efficiency gains, but also for further coherence and credibility. Cost reductions cannot be short-sighted and must lead to increased system-wide coherence and efficiency gains. Which actions is UN Women taking to further consolidate and improve joint business operations within the wider UN system? And could UN Women elaborate How they will keep member states informed of how current cost reduction measures are impacting further co-location and consolidation. Second, transparency and accountability are key to improving performance. We therefore note with concern that the Secretary General has signaled that progress in implementing the management and accountability framework has stalled. How will UN Women ensure improved implementation of the framework? Third, the dual reporting model is not yet sufficiently implemented, especially the number of resident coordinators that are requested to provide input on performance appraisals of heads of agencies lag behind. Could UN Women share what challenges you are facing in this regard? And since we would like to see full participation in this model, what can the Board do to facilitate compliance? Fourth, the system-wide evaluation on progress towards a new generation of UN Country Teams confirms that RC's estimates that 79% of entity-specific programming instruments are aligned with the cooperation framework. However, this alignment is very soft and does not translate into genuine derivation from the cooperation frameworks into agency-specific plans. We reiterate the importance of ensuring derivation of strategic notes from the cooperation frameworks. We request all agencies, including UN Women, to attach to each strategic note the confirmation from the respective RC of derivation from the respective cooperation framework. Fifth, last year the Board requested agencies to take further steps to ensure effective information sharing with RCs. We are pleased to note improvements in this regard. However, more work needs to be done to keep RCs better informed on agencies' outreach to funding partners. How does UN Women plan to improve this? And finally, preliminary findings of the system-wide evaluation indicate that, while more and more countries' configuration exercises are undertaken, they have not created a more tailored, needs-based country presence, and this is concerning. We call on all agencies, including UN Women, to connect ongoing business model reviews and reorganization exercises to the goal of needs-based country presence, rather than treat these processes in isolation. Madam President, Madam Executive Director, we acknowledge that there has been a lot of progress. However, in light of the current challenges and in the context of UN80, we call on all UN entities to go the extra mile together, to increase collaboration, joint programming, and integrated approaches in an ultimate effort in this last stretch to achieve the SDGs. I thank you.
I thank the distinguished representative from the Kingdom of the Netherlands for his comments, and there are no further speakers on the list, and I therefore invite the Secretariat to respond.

We take some of the points as advice and guidance and others which require specific information. I will respond to 2 elements and then request to respond to the question related to efficiencies and how we can maximize on back office services within the UN system and joint business operations, and we'll request our Deputy Director for Coordination Division, Madam Alice, to then respond to the other issues.

Thank you, Madam President, Ambassador Nicolas Klaas, our able and steadfast President. Good morning to you all. Excellencies, distinguished delegates, esteemed colleagues, it is an honor to update you today on our continued action to prevent and respond to sexual exploitation and abuse, SEA, and sexual harassment, SH. UN Women remains steadfast in every country where we serve, in every space we operate. We carry this mission with urgency and with care. Because this is not only a moral imperative, it is a matter of trust— the trust of the women and girls we serve, especially those living through crises, conflict, and systematic inequality. We act across 5 fronts: prevention, response, accountability, partnership, and cultural change. Each one essential, each one interlinked. Excellencies, let me share our internal progress. Over the past year, we strengthened safeguards to ensure reporting mechanisms are trusted, accessible, and centered on the needs of survivors. The 2024 UN System Perceptions Survey shows that over 90% of UN Women personnel know how and where to report SEA and SH. This is encouraging, but it is not enough, and we will continue to strive to ensure that 100% of our workforce know how and where to report. We are also becoming more precise in how we prevent. Today, 98% of our risk owning units are integrating SEA and SH risks into their assessments. This allows us to anticipate where harm may occur and to act before it does. To reinforce accountability, we operationalized a hybrid investigation model. It complements OIOS with internal capacity, ensuring timely appropriate responses. Beyond our own walls, we are also deepening engagement with the communities we serve. Our SEA focal points are active in every duty station. They are raising awareness, sharing tools, and helping communities navigate what can feel like an overwhelming system. A new outreach guide tailored for civil society and local actors is now in use. Step by step, we are closing the distance between policies and people. Excellencies, in 2024, we reached several critical milestones. We helped shape the first-ever SEA and SH indicator under UN SWAP 3.0. It is evidence-based, survivor-centred, and aligned with the Gender Equality Acceleration Plan. We are preparing to transition to ClearCheck 2.0, expanding vetting to include racism, racial discrimination, and other forms of misconduct. And in 2025, we will pilot the Misconduct Disclosure Scheme as per Executive Board direction— another step forward in due diligence and accountability. UN Women is also helping lead system-wide efforts. As a member of the UN Executive Group to Prevent and Respond to Sexual Harassment, we lead the work stream on knowledge sharing and collaboration, the backbone of policy coherence across the system. As part of this engagement, UN Women is responsible for key deliverables, including the UN system-wide knowledge hub on addressing sexual harassment, and an upcoming assessment informed by input from 36 members of the Executive Group, more than 120 UN system gender focal points, and external partners. We also support solutions beyond the UN, from Safe Cities, gender-responsive policies with WHO and UNODC, to joint policy advocacy with UNESCO and ILO. Whether in the world of work, sport, or the digital space, we help partners build safer environments and stronger systems of redress. Let me end where I began, with resolve. We will continue to deliver on this agenda with clarity, with accountability, and with dignity. Thank you to the Executive Board for your steadfast partnership. Together, we will uphold the trust placed in us, and we will work to ensure safety, dignity, and justice for all. I thank you.

Thank you very much for your comprehensive presentation, Madam Executive Director. Thank you, Madam President. We would like to thank UN Women for its continued efforts on ensuring the protection from and response to sexual exploitation, abuse, and sexual harassment. Important steps have been taken to reinforce a victim-survivor-centered approach and zero tolerance for SIA, and we underline the continuous key role of leadership in setting the tone at the top. Additionally, we welcome the efforts of UN Women to ensure an inclusive diverse and safe organizational culture in order to help address the root causes of SIA. We will ask some specific questions on the information shared in the report, but first, Madam Chair, we would like to discuss the bigger picture. With current funding cuts leading to resource constraints, we understand that prioritization decisions must be made. In our view, protecting and serving marginalized populations should remain essential and should be treated as a core function and responsibility rather than as an optional activity. We therefore expect UN agencies to protect hard-won gains and prioritize the prevention and response to SIA. This includes ensuring that sufficient resources, both human and financial, are structurally made available to effectively prevent and respond to SIA, especially at the country level. We know that SIA risks are likely to be increasing as funding goes down. So how will the United Nations Women ensure SIA prevention and response? Funds continues to improve amidst funding pressures. Collective action to streamline work, reduce duplication and fragmentation, and realize efficiencies is more relevant than ever. Further resource pooling, collective tools, and harmonized approaches can be instrumental in achieving further efficiencies and impact. Interagency collaboration on, for example, risk analysis, community engagement, and implementing partner capacity assessment and training are positive examples. Overall, where does UN Women see further opportunities for interagency collaboration in a manner that is both efficient and effective? Additionally, we would like to emphasize the importance of drawing from existing expertise within agencies and the system as a whole, specifically on GBV. Victim survivors of SIA suffer from the same root causes and are in need of the same services. Therefore, the mapping and further expansion of GBV services, especially in those areas where services are not easily accessible, would be very helpful. Beyond UN interagency efforts, broader multi-stakeholder tools and resources such as a common approach to protection from SIA and the misconduct disclosure scheme can also help. Noting the positive signals in the UNSG's 2025 Special Measures Report on both CAP-SIA, and we encourage all UN agencies to consider Formally endorsing it. It is noted that a 2024 PSEA perception survey was conducted, which provided insights into SEA-related issues and broader aspects of organizational accountability. Could UN Women share what the most important outcomes of this survey have been and what areas of improvement were identified based on this survey? We therefore welcome a continued dialogue on what is working and what can be improved and continue to support UN Women in its work on SIA. I thank you very much.

And I just thought it might be relevant to share a little bit more detail, because it links very much to the issues that you have just in your joint statement raised. One other— on a very positive note, I want to share that we are hosting the UN system-wide Knowledge Hub on addressing sexual harassment. We have had this in place for a couple of years now. We have recently made enhancements to it, such as translating the hub into the 6 official UN languages, and we also improved the accessibility for persons with disabilities. We've been promoting the platform, and actually that resulted in a record-high 16,000 clicks now in May. And this is very much also demonstrating what we have as part of the work stream in our discussions with the members of the Executive Group and also with the Gender Focal Point. Plus, in our conversations with partners outside the UN system— multilateral development organizations, financing organizations, civil society, private sector partners— we've been pulling together both on the challenges as well as opportunities. And we are, as part of the Executive Group, we are in the process of putting together a report that we will be discussing in detail in the Executive Group. This report will have a comprehensive assessment as well as clear, actionable recommendations. It will provide insights on current policies, tools, practices, and also identify key challenges and capacity gaps. We've looked at key tools and policies like the UN System Model Policy, the Code of Conduct, the ClearCheck Manager's Guide, the victim-centered approach, as well as the Knowledge Hub, and how they are being used across the UN system. In the feedback that we have received, most of our agency partners are applying the tools, but there is a variety how they are being applied depending on the agency, on location, and also the type of personnel. Common issues include limited coverage for some of the non-staff, like consultants; in some cases, outdated policies across the UN system that may not reflect the latest standards; unclear guidance that may make the tools hard to use; and in some cases, low awareness of the personnel. Important element that comes across the feedback that we have received, his persistent fear of retaliation, and in some cases inconsistent leadership support, then of course weakens trust and accountability. But at the same time, there are very promising practices across the UN system, and these practices are also demonstrating that real progress is achievable when the tools are up to date, when they are made accessible, accessible, they are tailored to the real needs, and when there is strong leadership and clear communication in place. So I want to just highlight that as an update to you, because this is an example, really, of agencies coming together, of strong interagency collaboration to take this critical issue forward. A key proposal that is emerging from this report is indeed, to look at how we are integrating the work on prevention of sexual harassment and prevention of sexual exploitation and abuse within a unified survivor-centered framework. And we will have a dedicated discussion in the Executive Group to discuss that further. So I just want to give that broader example for how the UN system as a whole is working and how UN Women is contributing to that critical work.

Thank you.

So that support and relationship that we have with the member states in supporting member states for the critical institutional support and that is capacities that are necessary is very, very important. very important for us, and equally the reporting that we expect from our partners when we work with them, to say our partners in their reporting, can they provide further information on any instances. Thank you, Madam President. I wanted to address specifically a few questions that were raised as part of the joint statement. On the funding question, UN Women remains fully committed to prioritizing PSEA— response to PSEA-SH, and will continue to ensure that the work is sustainably resourced. In this context, we are also recruiting. We had a vacant position of our PSEA-SH specialist. We are continuing to finalize the recruitment for that position as a priority. Addressing SCASH is also key to strengthening our organizational culture, and it will continue to remain a strategic priority under our strategic plan. On the question regarding the rollout and the pilot of the misconduct disclosure scheme, indeed, as we have committed, that 2025, we will be rolling out as a pilot both the MDS and we will also be transitioning to ClearCheck 2.0, which has an expanded scope in terms of the misconduct that it covers, in terms of the reporting. And of course, drawing on the lessons learned after the pilot and considering the capacity and the resource requirements for such, we will also explore feasibility of a broader rollout beyond— I mean, in terms of once we have done the pilot. So that was on the MDS rollout. There was a question on the perception survey. The PSEA perception survey, as you are aware, is led by the Office of the Special Coordinator, and the primary purpose of that survey is to help organizations assess how effective their efforts are are in preventing and responding to SEA and also identifying persistent challenges. As was noted in the statement by our Executive Director, we had a positive outcome through the survey results. 4.

Request UN Women to contribute to the United Nations Country Team Configuration Exercises and the implementation of their outcomes, to ensure that its presence at the country level is tailored to meet the specific challenges, priorities and needs of Programme Countries. 5. Request UN Women to intensify its effort to contribute to system-wide and interagency efficiencies, including through expanding the use of global shared services, common back offices and common premises, prioritizing the most cost-effective and resource-efficient efforts. 6, further requests UN Women to continue to pay in full its cost-sharing contributions in support of the Resident Coordinator System. 7, recalls Decision 2022/6 and 2024/7 and requests UN Women to take further steps to ensure its strategic notes are derived from the cooperation frameworks including: a) to attach to each strategic note the Resident Coordinator's confirmation of alignment with the cooperation framework, and b) to inform the Resident Coordinator in a timely manner of new programs and financial agreements signed to implement the strategic note, in line with the management and accountability framework.
